awd_titl_txt: A Learning Ecosystem for Teaching High School Students Machine Learning Concepts and Data Science Skills in Healthcare and Medicine
awd_abstract_narration:
Healthcare is rapidly changing into a multidisciplinary field. Data science and artificial intelligence (AI) have become integral for healthcare and medical services. Machine Learning (ML), a branch of AI, is broadly applicable for developing predictive models that drive research, development and healthcare practices. Unintentional bias within the datasets and computer programs used for ML creates healthcare outcomes which benefit some people more than others. This project will develop an innovative and inclusive learning and teaching ecosystem for high school students. The ecosystem consists of educational agencies and teachers, cross-disciplinary expertise from data scientists and medical clinicians, community members and college students from diverse background as mentors. Authentic cross-cultural discussions amongst community members and students will be a key component of students’ learning experience.  The ecosystem will provide a data science and ML laboratory course and an annual datathon. Computer science teachers will facilitate the course, and will also receive professional development in problem-based data science approaches. Students in the course will explore student-led, inquiry-based strategies on how to navigate and visualize large healthcare sets using the same programming languages and tools that data scientists use. During the datathon, students will team with their local community members and Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) teachers to solve authentic data-driven healthcare issues which are important and personal to them. Community members will share their experiences to ensure all voices are heard. Datathon participants will be introduced to culturally-responsive methods. The project is funded by the Innovative Technology Experiences for Students and Teachers (ITEST), which seeks to engage underrepresented students in technology-rich learning environments, including skills in data literacy, and increase students’ knowledge and interest in information and communication technology (ICT) careers.

During the project period, researchers will develop and study a semester-long program that engages up to 1000 Rhode Island high school students, with an emphasis on recruiting racial minorities and young women from 12 Title 1 schools. The researchers will investigate how students engage in the program and datathon, the usability and sustainability of this program, and the enactment of the innovative learning ecosystem. The following questions will guide this study: 1) How do the data laboratory and datathon contribute to student learning and efficacy in data science, and their interest in data science and healthcare careers? 2) What are teachers’ perspectives about the usability and effectiveness, including challenges, of the materials, curriculum, and supports? 3) How do teachers take up and enact the activities and tools to support student learning and interests in data science? Researchers will collect and analyze data using mixed methods, including data from a digital learning platform, surveys, interviews, assessments, and observations. The outcome will include a novel pedagogy for teaching high school students about rapidly evolving technologies. Deliverables will consist of annual professional development for the teachers; a public website for all Rhode Island district leaders, teachers, and parents; a vetted data science and ML laboratory course; and designs of the multidisciplinary, cross-cultural datathon. These will be freely shared and promoted online, presented at professional conferences, and published as research articles in peer-reviewed literature.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Data science and artificial intelligence (AI) are upending the way healthcare is delivered. Machine learning (ML), a branch of AI, is critical for accurately developing predictive models that drive research, development, and healthcare practices. In response to this challenge, A Learning Ecosystem for Teaching High School Students Machine Learning Concepts and Data Science Skills in Healthcare and Medicine developed and researched a novel pedagogy for teaching high school students about AI and data science in the context of healthcare.

The goals of the project, called Data Science, AI and You (DSAIY) in Healthcare for short, were to equip students to navigate complex STEM issues; encourage collaboration between students, educators, researchers, clinicians, and local stakeholders; and to prepare students for STEM jobs in fields with a scarcity of skilled workers.

The project adapted an undergraduate science course taught by Co-PI Celi at MIT and redesigned it for high school instruction within science, biomedical, engineering, computer science, and general STEM classrooms. The curriculum was developed to align with state and national computer science and science standards, including the Next Generation Science Standards. Delivered through the Scoutlier learning platform, the curriculum incorporated a number of technologies, including CODAP for data analysis and visualization of curated healthcare datasets; Code.org, Python, Google Colab, and Teachable Machine for coding; and hands-on health-related activities, such as the use of pulse oximeters. Students organized data; created and interpreted histograms, boxplots, and scatterplots; examined relationships among variables; and explored model training, testing, overfitting, cross-validation, bias, uncertainty, and responsible AI use. A two-day in-person capstone datathon/AI-a-Thon event focused on rapidly evolving issues related to large language model reliability, prompt design, source verification, unsupported claims, sycophancy, uncertainty, bias, and safety.

The project investigated how a socially meaningful healthcare context can support high school students’ learning of complex data science and AI concepts. DSAIY offered teacher professional learning with follow-up bimonthly support and feedback meetings. Through iterative co-refinement with 12 Rhode Island teachers, DSAIY reached over 560 students. The differentiated and scaffolded curriculum enabled students with limited prior subject knowledge or programming experience to collect and analyze data, interpret visualizations, examine machine learning processes, and evaluate AI-generated outputs.

Analyses of course assessments found improved performance in foundational machine learning concepts, although changes in self-efficacy and career awareness were modest or mixed across classrooms. Scoutlier analytics revealed differences in time on task, lesson completion, response patterns, and collaboration, indicating that teacher enactment and classroom context strongly influenced student engagement. Interviews and observations showed that specific curriculum components, including authentic data, collaborative problem solving, immediate visual feedback, and interactions with AI, data science, and medical professionals, helped students connect course concepts to real-world careers.

Research findings documented the importance of teacher effects and identified needs for additional support in graph interpretation, statistics, coding, healthcare terminology, and working with complex datasets. These findings guided revisions that added interactive machine learning activities, classroom posters, print and offline resources, differentiated lessons, stronger graphing supports, and redesigned AI-a-Thon investigations. The workforce events evolved from professional-led data challenges into experiences in which students tested AI systems, documented evidence and limitations, and developed conclusions with teachers and mentors. A pulse oximeter investigation was a particularly effective instructional anchor that connected measurement error to data quality, healthcare disparities, downstream model performance, and potential patient consequences. At the AI-a-Thon, students’ recognition of AI bias, sycophancy, and confident but incorrect answers increased, and dialogue analyses showed reciprocal learning with mentors taking up and extending students’ ideas. The project also developed and psychometrically examined a course-specific machine learning assessment, one of few designed for secondary students, and contributed evidence on the opportunities and challenges of implementing AI and data science curricula across settings that varied in location, students' socioeconomic backgrounds, classroom sizes, and prior knowledge.

DSAIY broadened participation by reaching students in urban, suburban, and rural public, private, charter, and career and technical education settings, including many who might not otherwise enroll in computer science. Its multigenerational “Hive Learning Ecosystem” enabled students and teachers to co-learn with clinicians, data scientists, AI experts, and undergraduate and graduate mentors. Several teachers implemented the curriculum across multiple semesters and planned to continue using it beyond this program’s support. Major products included the 18-lesson curriculum; Scoutlier-based lessons; CODAP, Python, Teachable Machine, and pulse oximeter activities; teacher implementation supports; student surveys and assessments; engagement-analysis methods; and a reproducible workflow for analyzing team dialogue; and replicable datathon/AI-a-Thon materials.

Findings were disseminated through publications, presentations at regional, national, and international conferences, public websites, media coverage, and shared curriculum resources. DSAIY offers a scalable model for integrating data literacy, AI literacy, ethical reasoning, teacher professional learning, and workforce exploration while preparing young people to become critical and responsible users and future developers of AI technologies.

More information about the project, including publications, can be found at https://www.dsaihealthed.org/ and https://concord.org/our-work/research-projects/dsaiy/
